[2025 summer phd math-stat — problem 1]

Part III, Problem 1 (25 pts). Let $X_1, \dots, X_n$ be i.i.d. from a one-parameter exponential family $p(x \mid \theta) = h(x)\exp\{\eta(\theta) T(x) - B(\theta)\}$, with $\eta(\theta)$ monotonically increasing and $\sum_i T(X_i)$ continuous.
(i) Construct the UMP test for $H_0 : \theta \le \theta_0$ vs $H_1 : \theta > \theta_0$.
(ii) Prove the test in (i) is uniformly most powerful.
(iii) Prove or disprove the existence of a UMP test for $H_0 : \theta = \theta_0$ vs $H_1 : \theta \ne \theta_0$.

response.text:
Let \(0<\alpha<1\) be the prescribed significance level, and write

\[
S_n=\sum_{i=1}^n T(X_i).
\]

The joint density is

\[
p_\theta^{(n)}(x_1,\dots,x_n)
=\prod_{i=1}^n h(x_i)\exp\{\eta(\theta)S_n-nB(\theta)\}.
\]

For \(\theta_2>\theta_1\),

\[
\frac{p_{\theta_2}^{(n)}(x)}{p_{\theta_1}^{(n)}(x)}
=\exp\{[\eta(\theta_2)-\eta(\theta_1)]S_n-n[B(\theta_2)-B(\theta_1)]\},
\]

which is an increasing function of \(S_n\), since \(\eta\) is increasing. Thus the family has a monotone likelihood ratio in \(S_n\).

---

## (i) UMP test for \(H_0:\theta\le \theta_0\) vs. \(H_1:\theta>\theta_0\)

Let \(F_{\theta_0}\) denote the CDF of \(S_n\) under \(\theta_0\). Since \(S_n\) is continuous, choose \(c_\alpha\) such that

\[
P_{\theta_0}(S_n>c_\alpha)=\alpha.
\]

Define the test function

\[
\phi_\alpha(X_1,\dots,X_n)
=
\mathbf 1\{S_n>c_\alpha\}.
\]

Equivalently, the rejection region is

\[
\boxed{\; \sum_{i=1}^n T(X_i)>c_\alpha \;}
\]

where \(c_\alpha\) is chosen so that the test has size \(\alpha\) at \(\theta_0\).

Because the likelihood ratio is increasing in \(S_n\), upper-tail probabilities are increasing in \(\theta\). Hence for every \(\theta\le \theta_0\),

\[
P_\theta(S_n>c_\alpha)\le P_{\theta_0}(S_n>c_\alpha)=\alpha.
\]

Thus \(\phi_\alpha\) has level \(\alpha\) for the composite null \(H_0:\theta\le \theta_0\).

---

## (ii) Proof that the test is UMP

Fix any \(\theta_1>\theta_0\). Consider the simple-vs-simple problem

\[
H_0:\theta=\theta_0
\qquad\text{vs.}\qquad
H_1:\theta=\theta_1.
\]

The likelihood ratio is

\[
\Lambda_{\theta_1,\theta_0}(X)
=
\frac{p_{\theta_1}^{(n)}(X)}{p_{\theta_0}^{(n)}(X)}
=
\exp\{[\eta(\theta_1)-\eta(\theta_0)]S_n-n[B(\theta_1)-B(\theta_0)]\}.
\]

Since \(\theta_1>\theta_0\), we have \(\eta(\theta_1)>\eta(\theta_0)\), so \(\Lambda_{\theta_1,\theta_0}\) is increasing in \(S_n\). Therefore the Neyman–Pearson most powerful level-\(\alpha\) test rejects for large values of \(S_n\), i.e.

\[
S_n>c_\alpha,
\]

where \(c_\alpha\) is determined by

\[
P_{\theta_0}(S_n>c_\alpha)=\alpha.
\]

This is exactly the test constructed in part (i).

Now let \(\psi\) be any other level-\(\alpha\) test for the composite null \(H_0:\theta\le \theta_0\). Then in particular,

\[
E_{\theta_0}[\psi]\le \alpha.
\]

By the Neyman–Pearson lemma, for the simple alternative \(\theta_1>\theta_0\),

\[
E_{\theta_1}[\psi]\le E_{\theta_1}[\phi_\alpha].
\]

Since \(\theta_1>\theta_0\) was arbitrary, this inequality holds for every \(\theta_1\in H_1\). Therefore \(\phi_\alpha\) has power at least as large as every other level-\(\alpha\) test at every point of the alternative.

Hence

\[
\boxed{\phi_\alpha=\mathbf 1\{S_n>c_\alpha\}}
\]

is uniformly most powerful for

\[
H_0:\theta\le \theta_0
\qquad\text{vs.}\qquad
H_1:\theta>\theta_0.
\]

This is the Karlin–Rubin theorem in this one-parameter exponential family setting.

---

## (iii) Existence of a UMP test for \(H_0:\theta=\theta_0\) vs. \(H_1:\theta\ne\theta_0\)

Assume \(\theta_0\) is an interior point of the parameter space, so that there exist both \(\theta_-<\theta_0\) and \(\theta_+>\theta_0\). We show that, for nontrivial \(0<\alpha<1\), no UMP level-\(\alpha\) test exists.

Suppose, toward contradiction, that a UMP level-\(\alpha\) test \(\phi\) exists.

First consider the simple alternative \(\theta_+>\theta_0\). As above, the likelihood ratio

\[
\frac{p_{\theta_+}^{(n)}}{p_{\theta_0}^{(n)}}
\]

is increasing in \(S_n\). Therefore, by the Neyman–Pearson lemma, the unique most powerful level-\(\alpha\) test rejects for large \(S_n\):

\[
\phi_+(X)=\mathbf 1\{S_n>c_\alpha\},
\]

where

\[
P_{\theta_0}(S_n>c_\alpha)=\alpha.
\]

Since \(\phi\) is assumed UMP, it must be most powerful against this particular \(\theta_+\). Hence, by uniqueness in the Neyman–Pearson lemma,

\[
\phi=\phi_+
\quad P_{\theta_0}\text{-a.s.}
\]

Now consider the simple alternative \(\theta_-<\theta_0\). Then

\[
\frac{p_{\theta_-}^{(n)}}{p_{\theta_0}^{(n)}}
=
\exp\{[\eta(\theta_-)-\eta(\theta_0)]S_n-n[B(\theta_-)-B(\theta_0)]\}.
\]

Since \(\eta(\theta_-)<\eta(\theta_0)\), this likelihood ratio is decreasing in \(S_n\). Thus the Neyman–Pearson most powerful level-\(\alpha\) test rejects for small \(S_n\):

\[
\phi_-(X)=\mathbf 1\{S_n<d_\alpha\},
\]

where

\[
P_{\theta_0}(S_n<d_\alpha)=\alpha.
\]

Again, because \(\phi\) is UMP, it must be most powerful against this particular \(\theta_-\), so uniqueness gives

\[
\phi=\phi_-
\quad P_{\theta_0}\text{-a.s.}
\]

Therefore we would need

\[
\mathbf 1\{S_n>c_\alpha\}
=
\mathbf 1\{S_n<d_\alpha\}
\quad P_{\theta_0}\text{-a.s.}
\]

But this is impossible for \(0<\alpha<1\) because the first test rejects in the upper tail of the null distribution, while the second rejects in the lower tail. Since \(S_n\) is continuous, these two rejection regions cannot coincide up to \(P_{\theta_0}\)-null sets.

Thus no nontrivial UMP level-\(\alpha\) test exists for the two-sided alternative.

Therefore,

\[
\boxed{\text{There is no UMP level-}\alpha\text{ test for }H_0:\theta=\theta_0
\text{ vs. }H_1:\theta\ne\theta_0,\quad 0<\alpha<1.}
\]

The only exceptions are trivial cases such as \(\alpha=0\) or \(\alpha=1\), or boundary cases where only one side of the alternative exists.
